lead: Knock in an SI engine happens when the end gas autoignites before the flame front reaches it. Whether knock occurs depends on how fast the end gas heats up and how long it waits. Three groups of factors control this: the fuel's resistance to autoignition, the engine's geometry and timing, and how the engine is operated. Changing any one factor can make knock stronger or weaker. Mechanics and drivers use this list to choose fuel, set spark timing and diagnose knock in a Chennai traffic jam or on a highway.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.3: knock and pre-ignition for the end-gas picture, and Chapter 3.2 for flame speed.

blocks.text: Octane number (ON) measures a fuel's resistance to autoignition. A higher ON means the end gas waits longer before it self-ignites, so knock is less likely. Some syllabi call ON the anti-knock rating. Fuel composition matters too: aromatics and iso-paraffins generally have high ON; normal paraffins have low ON. Petrol in India is sold as 91, 95 or 97 RON, where RON is the research octane number.

Mixture strength tells how far the actual fuel-air ratio is from the chemically correct one. It is written as the equivalence ratio φ = (F/A) ÷ (F/A)stoich, where F/A is the fuel-air ratio by mass and the subscript stoich means the chemically correct ratio. Knock tendency is highest for slightly rich mixtures, about φ = 1.05 to 1.15, which is an air-fuel ratio of roughly 13:1 — close to but richer than stoichiometric. Leaner mixtures (φ below about 0.9) knock less because less energy is released. Very rich mixtures (φ above about 1.2) also knock less because the excess fuel cools the charge and lowers the flame temperature.

blocks.where: φ is the equivalence ratio (no unit); F/A is the actual fuel-air mass ratio; (F/A)stoich is the stoichiometric fuel-air mass ratio, about 0.068 for petrol.

blocks.text: Compression ratio r = (Vs + Vc) ÷ Vc, where Vs is the swept volume and Vc is the clearance volume. A higher r squeezes the charge more, raising its pressure and temperature before the flame arrives. This makes the end gas hotter and closer to autoignition, so knock increases. Raising r from 8 to 10 in a petrol engine almost always increases knock unless the fuel's ON is raised.

Spark timing is measured in degrees before top dead centre (bTDC). Advancing spark, for example from 15° to 25° bTDC, starts combustion earlier. The peak pressure and temperature rise, and the end gas is compressed for a longer time before the flame reaches it. So more advance increases knock. Retarding spark reduces knock.

Combustion chamber shape controls flame travel distance and turbulence. A compact chamber with a central spark plug and good squish gives a short flame path and fast burning, which reduces knock. A long, narrow chamber or a side-mounted spark plug increases flame travel and knock. A larger bore also increases flame travel distance, so knock tends to rise with bore. Better cooling of the head and valves lowers metal temperatures and reduces hot spots that can trigger knock.

Speed affects knock through turbulence. As engine speed rises, air motion and flame speed increase. The flame crosses the chamber faster, leaving less time for end-gas reactions. So knock tendency generally decreases as speed increases from low to moderate values. Very high speeds can raise temperatures, but the dominant effect in most SI engines is that low-speed, high-load operation is the knock-prone zone.

Load is the throttle opening, which sets how much air-fuel mixture enters the cylinder. At higher load, the pressure and temperature inside the cylinder rise, so the end gas is hotter and knock increases. Coolant temperature also matters: raising coolant temperature from 80°C to 95°C makes the cylinder walls and the end gas hotter, so knock increases. Higher inlet air temperature has the same effect. Cooler intake air and cooler coolant both reduce knock.

These factors act together. A high-compression engine running at low speed, high load and hot coolant with advanced spark is the worst case. The same engine with high-octane fuel, retarded spark and cool coolant runs knock-free. The chamber shape chapter shows how geometry sets the flame travel that these factors act on.

examples.question: Classify each change as increasing or decreasing knock tendency: (a) compression ratio 8 to 10, (b) spark advanced from 15° to 25° bTDC, (c) coolant temperature 80°C to 95°C, (d) octane number 91 to 95.
steps: (a) Compression ratio rises from 8 to 10. Higher compression raises the pressure and temperature of the end gas before the flame arrives. The end gas reaches its autoignition temperature sooner. Knock tendency increases.

(b) Spark is advanced from 15° to 25° bTDC. Combustion starts earlier, peak pressure and temperature rise, and the end gas is compressed for a longer time before the flame front reaches it. Knock tendency increases.
(c) Coolant temperature rises from 80°C to 95°C. The cylinder walls and the end gas become hotter. The end gas needs less additional compression to autoignite. Knock tendency increases.
(d) Octane number rises from 91 to 95. Higher octane means the fuel resists autoignition for a longer time. The end gas waits longer before self-igniting. Knock tendency decreases.
examples.answer: (a), (b) and (c) increase knock tendency; (d) decreases knock tendency.

traps: A higher octane number reduces knock; a higher compression ratio or more spark advance increases knock. More is not always worse.
Advancing spark means moving the spark earlier (more bTDC). That increases knock. Retarding spark reduces knock.
Knock is worst at a slightly rich mixture near stoichiometric, not at the richest mixture. Very rich mixtures reduce knock.
Better cooling reduces knock. Raising coolant temperature from 80°C to 95°C increases knock, not decreases it.
A larger bore increases flame travel distance and knock. A compact chamber with a central spark plug reduces knock.

quiz.a: Octane number measures a fuel's resistance to autoignition. A higher octane number means the fuel resists knock better.

quiz.q: Why does advancing spark timing increase knock?
quiz.a: Advancing spark starts combustion earlier. Peak pressure and temperature rise, and the end gas is compressed for a longer time before the flame reaches it, so the end gas is more likely to autoignite.

quiz.q: An engine runs at compression ratio 9. If the ratio is raised to 11, what happens to knock tendency and why?
quiz.a: Knock tendency increases. A higher compression ratio raises the pressure and temperature of the end gas before the flame arrives, so the end gas reaches autoignition sooner.

quiz.q: Two identical engines run at 1500 rpm and 3000 rpm at the same load. Which is more likely to knock and why?
quiz.a: The engine at 1500 rpm is more likely to knock. At lower speed, turbulence and flame speed are lower, so the flame takes longer to cross the chamber. The end gas has more time to autoignite. At 3000 rpm, faster flame speed shortens the waiting time for the end gas.

quiz.q: Name two fuel factors and two engine design factors that affect knock.
quiz.a: Fuel factors: octane number and mixture strength. Engine design factors: compression ratio and spark timing (chamber shape and bore are also valid).

quiz.q: Explain why a very rich mixture reduces knock.
quiz.a: A very rich mixture has excess fuel. The extra fuel absorbs heat and lowers the flame temperature. Lower temperature means the end gas is less likely to reach autoignition, so knock reduces.

quiz.q: An engine knocks. Suggest two changes to reduce knock without changing the fuel.
quiz.a: Retard the spark timing and lower the coolant temperature. Retarding spark lowers peak pressure and temperature. Lower coolant temperature cools the cylinder walls and the end gas. Either change reduces knock.

quiz.q: Why does increasing coolant temperature increase knock?
quiz.a: Higher coolant temperature raises the cylinder wall temperature. The end gas receives more heat from the walls and starts at a higher temperature. It needs less compression heating to reach autoignition, so knock becomes more likely.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern cars use a knock sensor that retards spark before knock becomes audible. Direct injection cools the charge and allows higher compression ratios. Variable valve timing changes the effective compression ratio. Researchers study octane sensitivity, the difference between RON and MON, because it affects knock in downsized engines. Search for knock-limited spark advance and end-gas autoignition.
